doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Being called on unfamiliar tunes
summary: What a bassist does when a tune she doesn't know is called: ask, follow the piano, request a chart, and learn new songs on the gig.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well I’m trying to envision you going to one of your many gigs that are, not throw together is not the right word, but it’s not a working band, and someone calls a tune and you don’t know it.
Ah. Happens a lot. Happens a lot to me.
So what do you do? Do you say “can we not play that?”
You know, no I can’t do that. I’m the bass.
I know, you’re the bass player.

Right. I cannot. It happens a lot. Especially on gigs where you haven’t played with this person really ever, you know what I mean? But now they’re leading a set and they’re shooting, maybe you know this song but it’s really obscure to me. Very obscure. And so even if you’ve been doing this, like I have been professionally for 22 years now, and know quite a few songs, I still get stumped. There might be one or two songs in a set where I’m like what is that from 1910? I mean really, I can’t, with these crazy titles. And you’re like well sometimes, if it’s a complicated tune, I ask, is it easy or is it hard? If it’s easy my ears will guide me. If the piano player is playing a dominant line I know where it’s going. You know what I mean?
You hope, unless it’s sort of deceptive. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

If it’s a really hard tune with a lot of keys I’ll say, “Can you write it out for me.” If I don’t get a chance to then I’ve just got to help make this happen. And sometimes if I’m really not getting it I’ll be looking at him like what is it? That’s just one of the hardest things about being in the rhythm section. Because often the piano players will get to say if it’s too hard. The piano players are very vocal about that, oh I really don’t know it. The piano players don’t want to be showing up not knowing chords to the song. But then again if they do and you don’t know it, well then you’ve got to rely on them to teach it to you. Generally by the second chorus or third, generally after the head hopefully you have it. If it’s not the most difficult tune in the world. If it’s “Waltz for Debbie” and you’ve never played it, then you need a chart, I’m sorry, but you can’t really expect musicians to play a very difficult song that they haven’t heard before. That’s hard work.

And as far as a leader, it doesn’t serve the leader well either. Like I’m going to make you play it. Well okay but what you’re going to get you’re not going to be that happy with, it’s only going to reflect on you.

Yeah. You get to the bridge and you may not have any chords underneath you. Because they thought they knew the tune and then they get to the bridge and they start playing the bridge of another tune and, good luck. It happens.
And sometimes the piano player is waiting for you to hit the note.

Exactly. And I’ve guided just as many piano players. I’ve guided piano players on the top trying to teach tunes too. And it’s just that thing where we go okay, we’re here to learn. Music is about learning. And sometimes in those situations you go home with like, “I like that song we played, what was that called again?” And you actually go home with a new song that you might seek out and you might play again, and now you’ve learned it, on that gig. And that’s how it works for me.
